job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**Top priorities for Thursday:** (1) the Sec. 7(a)/7(b) conflict, which could end the prohibition after about 9.5 years; (2) the Sec. 3(c) "environmental assessment" carve-out; (3) the lack of any import or financing ban; (4) the unaddressed overlap with the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act; and (5) the missing enforcement hooks for Sec. 4.

1. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b), direct conflict (critical).** Section 7(a) keeps the prohibition in effect until Congress passes a joint resolution, but 7(b) says the entire Act ceases to have effect 10 years after enactment. Because Sec. 8 delays the effective date by 180 days, the prohibition could lapse after roughly 9.5 years in force.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), tonnage threshold.** The 10,000 metric ton/year threshold leaves everything below it outside the prohibition, including sustained operations labeled "pilot" or "test" mining. There is no cumulative or project-level limit.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "by a single vessel."** Operators could divide production across several vessels, each under the threshold, and avoid the definition entirely. Output should be aggregated across vessels, operators, affiliates, and contract areas.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), measurement.** The bill does not say whether the tonnage counts gross material (ore plus sediment) or only the mineral fraction, or whether "per year" means calendar year, a rolling period, or a permit period. "Recovery" is also undefined, so an operator could report only the processed nodules.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A), depth floor and undefined resource terms.** The 200-meter floor excludes shallower seabed mining, and it is unclear whether continental shelf activity is covered. "Mineral resources" and "other mineral resources" are undefined, so it is unclear whether sand, gravel, or hydrocarbons are included.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B), discretionary "Secretary" determination.** The bill does not say which Secretary decides, what "comparable" means, or what process, notice, or record applies. Because Sec. 5(b) criminal liability could rest on this determination, it also invites a vagueness challenge. Subparagraph (B) also measures risk, while the cross-reference to (A) measures volume, and the two don't line up.

7. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person."** Defining this as a citizen or a state-organized corporation excludes LLCs, partnerships, and trusts, and it does not reach foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. companies. The "anywhere" reach in Sec. 3(a) is therefore much narrower than it appears. Consider adding entities controlled by U.S. persons.

8. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel."** The 5,000 gross ton threshold and the phrase "equipped for the recovery" leave gaps. Smaller support vessels, seabed collector machines (which may not be vessels at all), and converted or re-flagged vessels could fall outside the Act. "Equipped" is also unclear as of when it is measured.

9. **Sec. 3(a), "engage in."** This phrase does not clearly reach financing, insurance, equipment or vessel services, offtake contracts, or processing. Companies could structure their involvement to stay outside it.

10. **Sec. 3(a), no import or sales ban.** The bill does not prohibit importing, buying, selling, or processing minerals recovered from the deep seabed. Without that, foreign-mined nodules could still enter U.S. supply chains, which is a major enforcement gap.

11. **Sec. 3(a), jurisdictional reach.** The bill does not address U.S.-flagged vessels owned by foreign persons, U.S.-flagged vessels on the high seas, or the Area beyond national jurisdiction. "In the United States" should be defined to include the EEZ and the outer continental shelf where intended.

12. **Sec. 3(b), "exploration license."** The term is undefined and no license regime is cited. The most likely referent is licenses issued under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA), but the bill should say so. As drafted, the grandfather covers "mining conducted under" such a license, not just exploration, so a pre-enactment exploration license could be used for commercial recovery with no volume cap or expiration.

13. **Sec. 3(b) and DSHMRA, unaddressed overlap.** The bill neither amends nor repeals DSHMRA, and it contains no "notwithstanding" clause. Under the canons favoring specific statutes over general ones and disfavoring implied repeal, a court could find that DSHMRA's licensing authority survives. The bill should expressly address this.

14. **Sec. 3(c), "environmental assessment" carve-out (critical).** This is undefined and has no limit on tonnage, duration, or sale of recovered material, and it requires no approved plan. It is the most obvious route for commercial-scale extraction under a testing label. The provision should cap volume, require approval and public disclosure, and bar sale of material beyond analytical samples.

15. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8, timing mismatch.** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the prohibition takes effect 180 days later. This creates ambiguity about what is unlawful during the gap and gives operators an incentive to accelerate activity and license issuance before the prohibition applies. The dates should be aligned, and the gap should be addressed.

16. **Sec. 4(a), registration.** The bill does not specify what information must be registered, the deadline, whether the information is public, or NOAA's rulemaking authority. "Operator" is also undefined.

17. **Sec. 4(b), quarterly reports.** The bill sets no required content (tonnage, location, depth, discharge, plume monitoring, incidents), no audit or verification, no public disclosure, and no filing deadline. Certification by the operator alone is weak.

18. **Sec. 4 has no enforcement hook.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register, failing to file, or filing a false certification carries no penalty. Add penalties for Sec. 4 violations and a false-statements provision.

19. **Sec. 5(a), civil enforcement mechanics.** The bill does not designate an enforcing agency, authorize injunctive relief or vessel seizure, include a citizen-suit provision, state a statute of limitations, or define how continuing violations are counted. Adding these would make the penalty more enforceable.

20. **Sec. 5(b), criminal liability.** "Willfully" is undefined, and there is no provision addressing individual officers or directors or forfeiture of vessels, equipment, or proceeds.

21. **Sec. 6, "shall seek to negotiate."** This creates no deliverable, no report to Congress, and no consequence if negotiations fail. It also does not say whether the domestic prohibition would continue, be modified, or lapse if a treaty is concluded.

22. **Sec. 7(a), lifting standard and NASEM report.** The bill does not require that the National Academies report be commissioned or set a deadline, and it does not say whether the report is a prerequisite to a joint resolution. "Serious harm" is undefined, so opponents could argue that any favorable report meets the standard. Also confirm that the joint resolution route is intended to require presentment to the President.

23. **Definitional gaps.** "Secretary" (used in Sec. 2, 6, and elsewhere), "seabed," "deep seabed," "recovery," "operator," "environmental assessment," and "exploration license" are all undefined or only partly defined. These undefined terms are the main source of avoidable litigation.

24. **No severability clause.** If a court strikes a provision such as Sec. 2(1)(B) or 2(2), the bill has no fallback. A standard severability clause should be added.

25. **No savings clause.** Nothing says that repeal or sunset does not affect liabilities already incurred. Given Sec. 7(b), this matters.

26. **No findings or purpose section.** The bill has no congressional findings on the seabed regime, environmental risk, or the basis for the U.S. reach. Findings would help a court defend the statute against international-law and extraterritoriality challenges, and they would help interpret terms such as "comparable" and "serious harm."

27. **International-law exposure.** The bill does not address the International Seabed Authority framework or the U.S. position as a non-party to UNCLOS. Foreign-sponsored contractors and their states may argue that the prohibition conflicts with the seabed regime. Sec. 6 does not resolve this.

**Verification notes:** I worked only from the text you pasted, which is described as the October 6 manager's amendment. Before the markup, compare it against the official committee print on congress.gov, since I can't confirm that this is the current version. My references to DSHMRA's license structure and to the current status of the ISA framework are from memory and should be checked by Senate legislative counsel or our policy team. Several of these fixes (especially 1, 13, and 15) are cleaner as technical amendments that the committee is more likely to accept.
